The narrow-gauge line from Pell to Tarsel climbs nine hundred metres in fourteen kilometres. It was built in 1911, and the curves its builders cut into the mountainside still carry the train up without a single slipped rail. A road reached the village in 1974, yet snow closes it every November, and until April the line is the only way in or out of Tarsel. In those months it carries everything the village needs.

Halfway up, at Gessen, the train pauses for six minutes so that the engine can take on water for the upper climb. While the tank fills, Tomas Brede, who keeps the halt, sets each sack of the council's winter coal on a scale and writes its weight in his book. The council pays for that coal every autumn before it spends money on anything else. Ilse Marran, who has driven the Hollin since 1996, leans from the cab to check her fire; the engine has worked the line since 1932. Above us goats pick their way across the scree slope.

Beyond Gessen the line runs below that slope, where a stone wall holds back the loose rock. The council rebuilt the wall in 2019 and paid for every stone from the village's own funds. Then comes the viaduct over the Lenn gorge, which visitors crowd the windows to photograph as the train rolls across. Ilse takes the Hollin over the arches so smoothly that the cups in the guard's van hardly rattle.

At Tarsel the cheese from the high farms is loaded for the run down to Pell, and the timetable is built around that trade: the first train leaves at dawn so that the farmers reach the Pell market by nine, and the visitors come up afterwards. In winter the same train brings up the post, the flour and the doctor.

I have ridden longer railways and grander ones, but none run with more skill than this one. Every curve, every arch and every sack of coal here is looked after by people who know exactly what it is for, and the village has come through thirty winters without missing a delivery.

Ostley's open-air pool opened in 1936 beside the Ost, with a diving tower at the deep end and a pike picked out in blue tiles on the basin floor. It closed in 2019, after a winter flood cracked the basin. The swimming club petitioned the council to put the tiles back under the water. Of the four designs entered, Teodora Lind's would cost the most and take two full summers to build, longer than any rival, but it was the only one that put the tiles back.

Lind had the tiles lifted one at a time and relaid on the floor of the new basin, pike and all. The swimming club had offered to buy them one by one if they had to go; Lind kept every one. The cracked old basin was crushed into the concrete of the new terrace, and beneath the terrace sits the café, its walls lined with timber from the old changing cubicles. The diving tower has been repaired out of the council's own budget, and a flood wall now stands between the basin and the river. Lind has done the hardest thing an architect can do, which is to let her own work disappear into somebody else's.

On opening day the swimming club swam the first length, and by noon the terrace was full. Under the terrace, a small bar sells tea and hot buttered toast to swimmers coming in from the water.

In the café hangs a photograph of opening day in 1936: boys crowding the tower, the swimming club posed on its steps, the terrace full in the afternoon sun, the Ost running a few yards from the edge, and the pike dark beneath the surface. Stand where the photographer stood today and, apart from the flood wall, you would struggle to say which picture is which.

Every choice Lind made, down to the colour of the grout, began with that photograph. Ostley has its pool back, rebuilt by someone who understood exactly what made it worth having.

For fifty years before this summer, the seven footbridges over the Askel were the colour of wet pavement. Now they are saffron, coral, teal, plum, lime, sky blue and tangerine. Residents voted online last spring to paint them, but the colours came from a class at Larch Street School, and Councillor Mara Varga carried the class's scheme to the council, which adopted it whole on the children's promise that people would find the right bridge at last.

The thinking behind that scheme is worth following step by step. Each bridge now wears the colour of the bus line that stops at its far end, so a commuter on the station steps can pick out her bridge by finding her bus's colour across the water. In 2019 the city planned to paint every bridge the same green; the children saw that seven matching bridges would be as hard to tell apart as the grey ones had been before. It is the cleverest piece of public design this city has produced in my lifetime, and it was drawn by eleven-year-olds.

The parks crew earned their share of the credit. Working from the class's chart, they painted between midnight and dawn so that every bridge stayed open, and before a brush touched the concrete they repaired each crack the inspectors had ringed in coloured chalk that spring, at a cost the council had set aside years ago. At the class's request they fixed boxes to the railings as well, and stock now blooms along all seven spans.

There was one mix-up, when the depot misread an order and sent the coral tins to the wrong bridge, and a wet July slowed the work, since paint will not take on concrete in the rain. Visitors now come down to the river to photograph the spans, but the real test comes at eight each morning, when commuters stream off the trains and cross to their buses without a second look.

The class deserves to see its scheme on every bridge Pellam builds from now on, and the crew has earned the thanks of everyone who crosses the Askel on the way to work.

passage:
Every June Kesterby closes Moss Lane to cars and sends its riders two kilometres uphill from the stone bridge, past the old chapel and the war memorial, to the green. Halfway up waits a bend named the Knuckle, a hundred metres of cobbled stones so steep that weaker riders climb off and push. Because of those stones, reaching the green at all counts as an achievement.

By custom Hettie Varn, the organiser, sounds the handbell for every rider who reaches the green, the last rider as long as the winner. The field included Arlo Maske, eleven times champion, whose first winning time, 9:41 in 1988, is still the record. Arlo has long told the pub that his 9:41 will stand as long as the hill. He leaves talk of a twelfth win to others. He had lifted sixteen-year-old Jory Penhale's old steel bicycle and called it heavy but fit for any hill. Before the start Arlo called the race anybody's, Jory and Nell Odrey included.

Jory passed Arlo just past the stone bridge and led him by the old chapel, up the Knuckle and under the war memorial to the green. His winning time of 9:58 was well outside the champion's record, and Nell Odrey finished third. By rule every rider climbs the Knuckle, and Pell's smooth farm track beside it stays gated. The last rider, nine-year-old Bea Tull, pushed her bicycle up the stones for twenty minutes, and Hettie swung the handbell for her as long as for Jory. That is the finest thing about the Moss Lane Climb: it gives the girl who walks up the stones the same cheer as the boy who wins.

Afterwards Arlo slipped his wedding ring back on, having handed it to his wife at the start. Moss Lane was laid with tarmac in 1964, all but the Knuckle, whose loose stones volunteers reset each spring, keeping it as firm as when the first race was run in 1961.

Most races end when the winner crosses the line. Kesterby's ends with the slowest rider, and with that one custom the village has built the fairest race I know.

March 2. Ms. Fenn says contest letters must be typed on a manual typewriter, with a deadline of Friday the thirteenth. Gran's old machine sits in her hall cupboard, its booklet still tucked inside the lid, and its keys left only pale dents. Dad was sure it would run and brought a can of oil from the garage, but my cousin Juno, who spent every summer at Gran's as a child, went straight to the ribbon.

March 4. Juno and I carried the machine to Mr. Ostrow, the old repairman on Keel Street. Mr. Ostrow asked our names. The model was new to him, but one look told him why it had stopped working: the ribbon had dried to a grey strip. Juno paid for a fresh ribbon still in its tin with her own pocket money, and all Mr. Ostrow wanted, he said, was to hear it type someday.

March 5. After that one visit to the old repairman, Juno and I fitted the ribbon at the kitchen table, Juno holding the spools while I wound, a two-person job, since on my own I would have tangled it. When the ribbon slipped a second time I wanted to give up, and Juno simply wound it back on. Dad tightened the carriage spring, which was still strong, and Juno swept the keys with my old paint brush. If I win, I will read my letter aloud in the capital in May, before the provincial council.

March 7. Mr. Ostrow had said the tin held his last ribbon of that size, and the cat has already knocked the machine sideways once. I typed my opening sentence, pulled the page out at once, and locked it in my desk drawer with the ribbon tin, where nothing could spill on either before Monday.

March 9. I posted the letter this morning, four days before the deadline. Juno set the margins for the envelope without a pause, the way Gran had shown her on rainy afternoons long ago. She says she will enter the contest herself next year. Then she carried the machine back to Gran's cupboard instead of asking to borrow it.
